metadata.title: Intrathecal baclofen therapy in stiff-man syndrome: a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
metadata.abstract: We performed a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of intrathecal baclofen (ITB) in stiff-man syndrome. Three patients, unresponsive to current therapy, received 50 micrograms of ITB or placebo on sequential days. Following ITB, all patients demonstrated improvement in reflex EMG activity. The mean reduction in total EMG activity (from all muscles) following stimulation of the medial plantar nerve (cutaneous flexor reflex) was 72% following 50 micrograms of ITB compared with 18% following placebo (ANOVA: significance of F, p < 0.0001). The mean latency to onset of the response was also significantly prolonged for all muscles following ITB (ANOVA: significance of F, p < 0.05). Although reflex EMG activity was reduced in all patients, clinical improvement was evident in only one patient, who differed from the others studied by a longer duration of disease, greater severity of stiffness, less fear of falling, and greater electrophysiologic improvement.

In.trathecal baclofen therapy
in stiff-man syndrome:
A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
P.L. Silbert, MBBS, FRACP; J.Y. Matsumoto, MD; P.G. McManis, MBBS, FRACP;
K.A. Stolp-Smith, MD; B.A. Elliott, MD; and K.M. McEvoy, MD, PhD

Article abstract-We performed a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of intrathecal baclofen (ITB) in stiff-man syndrome. Three patients, unresponsive to current therapy, received 50 pg of ITB or placebo on sequential days. Following
ITB, all patients demonstrated improvement in reflex EMG activity. The mean reduction in total EMG activity (from
all muscles) following stimulation of the medial plantar nerve (cutaneous flexor reflex) was 72% following 50 pg of ITB
compared with 18% following placebo (ANOVA: significance of F, p < 0.0001). The mean latency to onset of the response was also significantly prolonged for all muscles following ITB (ANOVA: significance of F, p < 0.05). Although reflex EMG activity was reduced in all patients, clinical improvement was evident in only one patient, who differed from
the others studied by a longer duration of disease, greater severity of stiffness, less fear of falling, and greater electrophysiologic improvement.
NEUROLOGY 1995;45:1893-1897

Stiff-man syndrome (SMS) is a r a r e disorder
characterized by involuntary stiffness of axial
and lower-extremity muscles with superimposed
painful muscle spasms.' The etiology is unknown, but a n immune-mediated mechanism is
suggested by the presence of antibodies t o glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) and the strong
association with other autoimmune diseases.2
GAD catalyzes the conversion of glutamate t o
GABA, and there are reduced CSF GABA levels
in some patients with SMS,3 making baclofen
(which acts on GABAB receptors) a logical therapy.
CSF penetration of baclofen is poor following
oral administration4 and, although effective in
some case^,^,^ the response in SMS is often variable and inadequate.7 Intrathecal administration
of baclofen avoids the high systemic levels required with oral administration because of limited
CSF p e n e t r a t i ~ n CSF
. ~ levels up to 50 times
higher may be achieved with ?booth of the oral
dose.* There are reports of intrathecal baclofen
(ITB) in five cases of SMSg-llbut most trials were
open, and there was no electrophysiologic monitoring of the effects of ITB. In the only reported patient with a blinded evaluation, no improvement
could be documented.ll We report a double-blind,
placebo-controlled trial of ITB therapy in three pa-

tients with SMS, with intensive clinical and electrophysiologic monitoring.
Methods. Patient selection. Three patients with SMS
were recruited for a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
of ITB therapy. The study was approved by the Mayo
Clinic Institutional Review Board. Patients were selected
because of inadequate control on their current therapy
due to lack of efficacy or side effects. Symptoms of SMS
had been present for 6 years in patient 1, 4 years in patient 2, and 10 years in patient 3, and these patients
were currently on combinations of diazepam, clonazepam, baclofen, valproate, and prednisone. All patients
fulfilled the clinical and electrophysiologic diagnostic criteria of Lorish et a17 and had positive anti-GAD antibodies. All patients had a n increased lumbar lordosis, reduced range of lumbar movement, paraspinal muscle hypertrophy, rigid abdominal muscles, spontaneous and
startle-induced spasms, and at least a partial response to
benzodiazepine therapy. Lower-extremity reflexes were
brisk in all patients, with asymmetry of the stiffness and
reflexes in patients 2 and 3. Informed consent was obtained and current medications were continued. The protocol allowed for patients to receive blinded intrathecal
administration of either 50 pg of baclofen or placebo on
day 1, with the other medication given on day 2. Following this, patients were eligible to receive a further trial of
either 75 or 100 pg of ITB with placebo control, as determined by the patient's subjective response and the observed clinical response to the lower dose.

Patient evaluation. Patients completed the following
evaluations before and after each intrathecal injection:
1. Patient self-evaluation. A self-evaluation of changes
in stiffness, spasms, mobility, and walking. Each of these
was rated as stable, or mildly (kl), moderately (*2), or
markedly (k3) improved or deteriorated relative to baseline, with a maximum score of *12. Patients were encouraged to assess themselves by doing activities known
to aggravate their symptoms. Evaluations were completed 90 minutes and 3% hours after the intrathecal injection, and the mean score was compared with a baseline 1 hour prior. The patient self-evaluation was also
completed on two occasions each day (11AM and 1PM) for
2 days prior t o the study.
2. Electrophvsioloeic evaluation. Reflex EMG activity
was assessed using the cutaneous flexor (exteroceptive)reflex obtained following medial plantar nerve stimulation
using a modification of the techniques of Meinck et all2 and
A train of three square-wave stimBrashear and Phi1li~s.l~
uli of 0.1-msecduration at 200 Hz was delivered to the medial plantar nerve on the medial edge of the plantar fascia
just proximal to the metatarsal head. We chose this site of
stimulation as it gave the maximal reflex response. The
bandpass was 20 to 2,000 Hz. The stimulus intensity was
1.5 to 1.75 times the motor threshold, as determined by the
presence of a toe twitch. Stimuli were delivered at intervals
of greater than 45 seconds to avoid habituation. Surface
EMG activity was recorded over the biceps brachii, triceps,
L-3 paraspinal muscles, lower rectus abdominis, biceps
femoris, rectus femoris, medial gastrocnemius, and tibialis
anterior muscles on the more symptomatic side. Recording
positions were maintained for the duration of the study.
Recorded muscle activity was rectified and three trials
were performed, each consisting of five averaged responses
(Nicolet Viking 11). The reproducibility of the response for
all muscles in all patients (between trials) was determined
by calculating the percentage variation from the mean for
each muscle in each patient and then overall. The latency
to onset was measured for each muscle, and the area under
the curve for all reflex EMG activity between 50 and 800
msec after the stimulus was recorded. The study was performed before and approximately 90 minutes following
each intrathecal injection.
3. Clinical evaluation. Muscle tone and stiffness were
assessed clinically using the Ashworth score, before and
approximately 2% hours following the intrathecal injection.14 This grades spasticity a s resistance to passive
movement on a five-point scale, where a score of 1 corre1894 NEUROLOGY 45 October 1995

sponds to no resistance, and rigidity in flexion or extension
gives a score of five. A videotaped evaluation was performed using a standard format on all patients before and
approximately 2 hours after intrathecal injection. Patients
were videotaped while walking, turning, sitting down, rising from a chair, bending forward, and standing. The preand post-injectionvideos were then evaluated by two experienced blinded examiners (K.M.M., K.A.S.) for mobility,
spasms, walking, stiffness, and overall function using the
same measures as for the patients’ self-evaluation.
For all evaluations, the pre- and post-injection assessments were compared on the given study day. The patients’ usual medications were given following the baseline assessments and a t least 2 hours prior t o the intrathecal injections. Times for administration of the patients’ usual medications, intrathecal injections, and subjective, objective, and electrophysiologic evaluations were
consistent between the study days.
Statistical analysis. Statistical significance between
groups was assessed by ANOVA and Wilcoxon’s signed
rank test for nonparametric variables. A p value of ~ 0 . 0 5
was considered significant.

Results. All intrathecal injections of baclofen were
performed without cardiorespiratory complications.
Patient self-eualuation. Patients 1and 2 noted an
improvement following placebo ( + 5 in patient 1and
+4 in patient 2), with a deterioration following ITB
(-3 in patient 1 and -1.5 in patient 2). The reported improvements following placebo were similar
t o the improvements they normally experienced
taking their usual oral medications on the days
prior to the trial ( + 3 for both patients). Following
ITB, these patients described feelings of unsteadiness of the legs and more difficulty walking. Patient
3 deteriorated following placebo ( - 6 ) and improved
following ITB ( + 8 ) . For patient 3, all individual
components of the subjective evaluation score improved. The placebo response was similar t o his
usual daily response (-4).The overall response to
ITB for all patients was not statistically significant.

14.6%. A treatment effect following intrathecal
placebo was evident as the patients' usual medications were continued throughout the study, and
were taken immediately after the baseline electrophysiologic studies on both days. The pre-injection
baseline reflex EMG activities for all patients were
similar on both days. The mean reduction in EMG
activity from all muscles for all patients was 72%
following ITB compared with 18%following placebo
(ANOVA: significance of F, p < 0.0001). All patients
had a lesser reduction in EMG activity following
ITB for the biceps and triceps muscles as compared
with the lower-extremity muscles. The reduction in
EMG activity following ITB was significant in the
lumbar paraspinal and lower rectus abdominis
muscles (ANOVA: significance of F, p < 0.021, biceps and rectus femoris muscles (ANOVA significance of F, p < 0.02>, and medial gastrocnemius
and tibialis anterior muscles (ANOVA: significance
of F, p < O.OOOl), but not the biceps and triceps. Patient 3 displayed a dramatic reduction (86%) in
total reflex EMG following ITB, compared with a
6% increase following placebo (figure). Patient 1
had a reduction in total EMG activity following
ITB of 52% compared with 31% following placebo,

and for patient 2 the reductions were 78% following
ITB and 30%following placebo.
For all muscles, the mean latency to onset of the
response following ITB was significantly prolonged
(table 2) (ANOVA significance of F, p < 0.05). The
change in onset latency was not significant for biceps and triceps, or for the medial gastrocnemius
and tibialis anterior muscles, but was statistically
significant for lumbar paraspinal and lower rectus
abdominis muscles (ANOVA: significance of F, p <
0.05) and biceps and rectus femoris (ANOVA: significance of F, p < 0.05).
Clinical evaluation. Stiffness. The Ashworth
score to assess tone and stiffness was unchanged
following placebo, but fell following ITB from Ashworth 3 t o Ashworth 2 for patients 1 and 2, and
from Ashworth 4 to Ashworth 3 for patient 3. These
changes were not statistically significant ip = 0.08).
Observer videotaDe evaluation. The mean improvement for patient 1 following intrathecal
placebo was +4.5 with a +0.5 improvement following ITB. The corresponding results for patient 2
were - 1following intrathecal placebo and - 1.5 following ITB. The results for patient 3 were 0 following intrathecal placebo and +7 following ITB.
These changes were not statistically significant.

Discussion. Despite our small sample size, we were
able t o detect a significant electrophysiologic response in SMS following ITB as evidenced by the reduction in total reflex EMG activity and prolongation
of the onset latency of the cutaneous flexor reflex.
The cutaneous flexor reflex is one of several exteroceptive reflexes consistently exaggerated in
SMS.12J3J5Presumably, these reflex abnormalities
reflect hyperexcitability along polysynaptic reflex
arcs, most prominently at the spinal level. We observed maximal reflex EMG activity following medial plantar nerve stimulation, and found that this
reflex could be reliably measured without habituation during the testing protocol, making it an excellent physiologic measure of SMS. Other electrophysiologic techniques are of limited value in evaluating the effects of treatments in SMS. Monosynaptic reflex arcs are usually normal,12 and although documentation of continuous muscle activOctober 1995 NEUROLOGY 45 1895

ity is useful in the initial evaluation of SMS, it may
be absent in rested patients on medical therapy.
This was apparent to us during the pretrial evaluation of our patients, and for this reason we did not
employ this technique during the trial.
Two aspects of the electrophysiologic response in
our patients bear further comment. The reflex
EMG activity was most markedly suppressed in
the legs and paraspinal muscles, consistent with
the known gradient of distribution of ITB following
lumbar intrathecal administration.EThis pattern of
response may also, i n part, reflect the known
greater hyperexcitability of t r u n k a n d lowerextremity muscles in SMS.15 The prolongation of
t h e onset latency i n t h e proximal leg a n d
paraspinal muscles cannot be explained with certainty, but most likely reflects reduced temporal
summation along the flexor reflex pathways due to
baclofen’s effects on presynaptic inhibition and
postsynaptic neuronal excitability.16J7 Together,
these findings suggest that ITB was acting in a
local and inhibitory manner at the spinal level.
Although muscle stiffness was reduced in all patients, we were unable to document a statistically
significant change. This may be due to a combination of the small sample size and lack of sensitivity
of the Ashworth scale. Although we observed an
electrophysiologic response to ITB in all patients,
only one responded with clear clinical improvement. This patient was more severely affected, had
asymmetric involvement of the lower extremities,
had a longer duration of disease, and also showed
greater electrophysiologic improvement following
ITB. An insufficient dose, or a n early peak CSF
level of ITB, may account for the lesser electrophysiologic improvement in the two patients who
did not respond, but both patients reported increased unsteadiness of their legs and more difficulty walking following ITB, despite a reduction in
muscle stiffness. We interpret these changes as
treatment effects, and, together with the patients’
“fear of falling,” we felt that, following unblinding
of the first stage of the trial, a higher dose of ITB
would not benefit these patients. In these patients
(and in future trials), further evaluation of the effects of ITB would best be performed using continuous intrathecal infusion through an intraspinal
catheter to allow time for adaptation and to adjust
the dose if necessary.
Brashear and Phillips13 previously noted the discrepancy between the electrophysiologic and clinical responses. Their patient’s subjective clinical response was significantly delayed in comparison
with the observed changes in reflex muscle activity
and muscle stiffness. This further supports our
suggestion that a period of time may be needed in
these patients to allow for adaptation to changes in
their muscle tone, and that the exteroceptive reflexes are a sensitive indicator of changes in reflex
pathways important in the pathophysiology of
SMS.
In previously reported patients receiving ITB for
1896 NEUROLOGY 45 October 1995

SMS, three showed an impressive response to longterm ITB.gJOPenn and Mangierig documented a response to an open test dose of 75 pg, although the
patient with advanced SMS, treated with a relatively limited dose of ITB (120 pg/d), showed longterm improvement in spasms and pain, but no
functional improvement because of lower-extremity
ankylosis. Ford and Fahnll reported a similar patient with advanced SMS, a relatively fixed increased lumbar lordosis, and ankylosis of the hips,
who showed no improvement following doubleblind administration of bolus test doses up to 100
bg. The pattern of response in these patients, together with t h e SMS patients reported in our
study, suggests that those most likely to benefit
from ITB are those with moderately severe disease,
but without a fixed deformity or ankylosis. Of the
three patients reported in our trial, patient 3 has
recently commenced continuous long-term ITB infusion and is responding well to his current dose of
730 pg/day. The other two patients have currently
elected to continue their prestudy drug therapy,
but may undergo further evaluation in the future
using continuous infusion of ITB through an intraspinal catheter.
In summary, our trial has demonstrated a significant electrophysiologic improvement in SMS following ITB. Although this supports the suggested
efficacy of ITB in SMS,gJothe overall response in
our patients did not always parallel the electrophysiologic improvement. Long-term clinical efficacy remains to be proven, but we believe that ITB may be
efficacious in reducing the stiffness and spasms in
some patients with SMS. Continuous infusion may
be preferable to bolus administration for assessing
the response to ITB in selected patients.

Patient evaluation. Patients completed the following

1. Patient self-evaluation. A self-evaluation of changes
in stiffness, spasms, mobility, and walking. Each of these
was rated as stable, or mildly (kl), moderately (*2), or
markedly (k3) improved or deteriorated relative to baseline, with a maximum score of *12. Patients were encouraged to assess themselves by doing activities known
to aggravate their symptoms. Evaluations were completed 90 minutes and 3% hours after the intrathecal injection, and the mean score was compared with a baseline 1 hour prior. The patient self-evaluation was also
completed on two occasions each day (11AM and 1PM) for
2 days prior t o the study.
2. Electrophvsioloeic evaluation. Reflex EMG activity
was assessed using the cutaneous flexor (exteroceptive)reflex obtained following medial plantar nerve stimulation
using a modification of the techniques of Meinck et all2 and

Discussion. Despite our small sample size, we were
able t o detect a significant electrophysiologic response in SMS following ITB as evidenced by the reduction in total reflex EMG activity and prolongation
of the onset latency of the cutaneous flexor reflex.
The cutaneous flexor reflex is one of several exteroceptive reflexes consistently exaggerated in
SMS.12J3J5Presumably, these reflex abnormalities
reflect hyperexcitability along polysynaptic reflex
arcs, most prominently at the spinal level. We observed maximal reflex EMG activity following medial plantar nerve stimulation, and found that this
reflex could be reliably measured without habituation during the testing protocol, making it an excellent physiologic measure of SMS. Other electrophysiologic techniques are of limited value in evaluating the effects of treatments in SMS. Monosynaptic reflex arcs are usually normal,12 and although documentation of continuous muscle activOctober 1995 NEUROLOGY 45 1895

ity is useful in the initial evaluation of SMS, it may
be absent in rested patients on medical therapy.
This was apparent to us during the pretrial evaluation of our patients, and for this reason we did not
employ this technique during the trial.
Two aspects of the electrophysiologic response in
our patients bear further comment. The reflex
EMG activity was most markedly suppressed in
the legs and paraspinal muscles, consistent with
the known gradient of distribution of ITB following
lumbar intrathecal administration.EThis pattern of
response may also, i n part, reflect the known
greater hyperexcitability of t r u n k a n d lowerextremity muscles in SMS.15 The prolongation of
t h e onset latency i n t h e proximal leg a n d
paraspinal muscles cannot be explained with certainty, but most likely reflects reduced temporal
summation along the flexor reflex pathways due to
baclofen’s effects on presynaptic inhibition and
postsynaptic neuronal excitability.16J7 Together,
these findings suggest that ITB was acting in a
local and inhibitory manner at the spinal level.
Although muscle stiffness was reduced in all patients, we were unable to document a statistically
significant change. This may be due to a combination of the small sample size and lack of sensitivity
of the Ashworth scale. Although we observed an
electrophysiologic response to ITB in all patients,
only one responded with clear clinical improvement. This patient was more severely affected, had
asymmetric involvement of the lower extremities,
had a longer duration of disease, and also showed
greater electrophysiologic improvement following
ITB. An insufficient dose, or a n early peak CSF
level of ITB, may account for the lesser electrophysiologic improvement in the two patients who
did not respond, but both patients reported increased unsteadiness of their legs and more difficulty walking following ITB, despite a reduction in
muscle stiffness. We interpret these changes as
treatment effects, and, together with the patients’
“fear of falling,” we felt that, following unblinding
of the first stage of the trial, a higher dose of ITB
would not benefit these patients. In these patients
(and in future trials), further evaluation of the effects of ITB would best be performed using continuous intrathecal infusion through an intraspinal
catheter to allow time for adaptation and to adjust
the dose if necessary.
Brashear and Phillips13 previously noted the discrepancy between the electrophysiologic and clinical responses. Their patient’s subjective clinical response was significantly delayed in comparison
with the observed changes in reflex muscle activity
and muscle stiffness. This further supports our
suggestion that a period of time may be needed in
these patients to allow for adaptation to changes in
their muscle tone, and that the exteroceptive reflexes are a sensitive indicator of changes in reflex
pathways important in the pathophysiology of
SMS.
In previously reported patients receiving ITB for
1896 NEUROLOGY 45 October 1995

SMS, three showed an impressive response to longterm ITB.gJOPenn and Mangierig documented a response to an open test dose of 75 pg, although the
patient with advanced SMS, treated with a relatively limited dose of ITB (120 pg/d), showed longterm improvement in spasms and pain, but no
functional improvement because of lower-extremity
ankylosis. Ford and Fahnll reported a similar patient with advanced SMS, a relatively fixed increased lumbar lordosis, and ankylosis of the hips,
who showed no improvement following doubleblind administration of bolus test doses up to 100
bg. The pattern of response in these patients, together with t h e SMS patients reported in our
study, suggests that those most likely to benefit
from ITB are those with moderately severe disease,
but without a fixed deformity or ankylosis. Of the
three patients reported in our trial, patient 3 has
recently commenced continuous long-term ITB infusion and is responding well to his current dose of
730 pg/day. The other two patients have currently
elected to continue their prestudy drug therapy,
but may undergo further evaluation in the future
using continuous infusion of ITB through an intraspinal catheter.
In summary, our trial has demonstrated a significant electrophysiologic improvement in SMS following ITB. Although this supports the suggested
efficacy of ITB in SMS,gJothe overall response in
our patients did not always parallel the electrophysiologic improvement. Long-term clinical efficacy remains to be proven, but we believe that ITB may be
efficacious in reducing the stiffness and spasms in
some patients with SMS. Continuous infusion may
be preferable to bolus administration for assessing
the response to ITB in selected patients.
